q: Wednesday evening club race, J/24s on a starboard-tack reach. Red is directly behind you; her bow is about a metre behind the line abeam of your transom. In the words of the rules, are you overlapped?
answer: No — Red is clear astern: her hull and equipment are behind a line abeam from the aftermost point of your hull
why: Definition Clear Astern and Clear Ahead; Overlap: a boat is clear astern when her hull and equipment are behind a line abeam from the other's aftermost point.

q: National championship, 470s beating on port tack. Blue has been sailing to leeward and slightly behind you; her bow has just moved ahead of the line abeam of your stern, about half a boat length to leeward. What is the state between you now?
answer: You are overlapped — neither boat is clear astern of the other, so rule 11 now applies between you
why: Definition Overlap: boats overlap when neither is clear astern — the moment Blue's bow crosses the line abeam your transom.

answer: No — on a beat boats on opposite tacks are not overlapped; the terms apply across tacks only when rule 18 applies or both sail more than 90° from the true wind
why: Definition Overlap: the terms apply to boats on opposite tacks only when rule 18 applies or both sail more than 90° from the true wind.

q: Melges 24s on the run in 15 knots. You are on starboard gybe, Blue on port gybe, both sailing dead downwind side by side about 20 m apart and slowly converging. Are you overlapped in the sense of the rules?
answer: Yes — both of you are sailing more than 90° from the true wind, so the overlap terms apply even though you are on opposite tacks
why: Definition Overlap: boats on opposite tacks are overlapped when both are sailing more than 90° from the true wind (rule 10 still governs them).

answer: Yes — equipment in its normal position counts, and an extended bowsprit with the sail set is in its normal position
why: Definition Clear Astern: judged by hull and equipment in normal position; a bowsprit extended with the sail set is equipment in normal position.

answer: At the moment Blue's bow and equipment dropped behind the line abeam your transom — an overlap exists only while neither boat is clear astern

answer: Yes — you could sail your course with no need to take avoiding action, which is what keeping clear means
why: Definition Keep Clear (a): the right-of-way boat can sail her course with no need to take avoiding action; no minimum distance is set.

answer: Yes — you can sail your course without taking avoiding action; keeping clear does not require any particular distance

q: On the run of a windward–leeward course in 12 knots you are in a 470 on port gybe, boom out to starboard. Grey is running on starboard gybe and converging slowly from your right, two hull lengths away; no mark is near. Who keeps clear?

why: Rule 10 applies on every point of sail; definition Tack: a boat is on the tack of her windward side, opposite to her boom.

answer: You — she is on port tack and you are on starboard; rule 10 applies regardless of who is beating or running
why: Rule 10: the port-tack boat keeps clear of the starboard-tack boat; there is no beating-over-running rule.

why: Rule 10: the port-tack boat keeps clear; ducking astern is the normal way to do it, and the starboard boat need not alter course.

why: Definition Clear Astern/Overlap: the terms apply to opposite tacks only under rule 18 or when both sail more than 90° from the wind.

why: Rule 10 does not depend on overlap; rule 12 (clear astern keeps clear) is only between boats on the same tack.

why: Rule 10 has no exception for size, speed or manoeuvrability: the port-tack boat keeps clear.

why: Rule 10 is about tacks and keeping clear; current, waves or a dying breeze never excuse the give-way boat.

why: Definition Keep Clear: the right-of-way boat must be able to sail her course with no need to take avoiding action.

q: You are on port tack a length from the finishing line, aiming to finish at the committee boat end. Blue is on starboard tack and will cross your path exactly at the line. You feel that a boat about to finish should be let through. Who keeps clear?
answer: You — the port-tack boat keeps clear of the starboard-tack boat right up to the finish (rule 10)
why: Rule 10 applies until a boat has finished and cleared the line; there is no priority for the boat about to finish.

q: On a reaching leg in 20 knots you are on starboard tack, heading for the gybe mark. Black, on port tack, has already rounded it and is coming back towards you on the reciprocal course; you are nearly head-on, two lengths apart. Black's crew hails «Keep right, like ships!». What must happen?
answer: Black keeps clear — the head-on rule of the collision regulations does not apply between boats racing; under rule 10 the port-tack boat keeps clear
why: Between boats racing, Part 2 replaces the IRPCS; on opposite tacks rule 10 decides, whatever the angle of approach.

q: In 25 knots and big waves you are ducking a starboard-tack boat on the beat. As you pass behind her a wave throws your bow into the corner of her transom. You tell her that the wave did it, not you. How does the rule see it?

why: Rule 10 and definition Keep Clear: the give-way boat must leave a margin that works in the existing conditions.

q: First beat of a Star class regatta in Split. You and Blue are both close-hauled on starboard tack and overlapped, Blue a length to leeward of you. You are slowly sagging down towards her. Who keeps clear?
answer: You — on the same tack and overlapped, the windward boat keeps clear (rule 11)
why: Rule 11: when boats are on the same tack and overlapped, the windward boat keeps clear of the leeward boat.

q: On a reach in a J/24 fleet Grey comes up from clear astern and establishes an overlap to leeward of you, about a length away, then holds her proper course. answer: Grey — once overlapped you are the windward boat and keep clear (rule 11); her overlap from astern only limits how high she may sail (rule 17)
why: Rule 11 puts the duty on the windward boat however the overlap began; rule 17 limits the leeward boat to her proper course.

answer: You — same tack and overlapped: the windward boat keeps clear, and a gust does not change that (rule 11)
why: Rule 11: the windward boat keeps clear; she must sail with a margin that allows for gusts and waves.

figure.note: A gust heels you down towards Yellow

ru.A gust heels you down towards Yellow: Порыв кренит вас и валит на Жёлтую

q: Both of you are running on starboard gybe in a Laser fleet, booms out to port, overlapped and a length apart. You are on Blue's starboard side — the side her boom is not on. Blue says you are the windward boat and must keep clear. Is she right?
answer: Yes — on a run the windward boat is the one on the side opposite the boom; you are to windward of Blue and keep clear (rule 11)
why: Definition Leeward and Windward: running, the leeward side is the side the mainsail lies on; the other side is windward (rule 11).

q: Thirty seconds before the start you are overlapped to windward of Green, both on starboard tack, reaching slowly along the line. Green luffs steadily towards head to wind to open a gap to leeward. You protest that she is sailing above her proper course. Must you respond?
answer: Yes — before the start there is no proper course, so Green may luff up to head to wind, giving you room to keep clear; you keep clear (rule 11)
why: Rule 11: the windward boat keeps clear; rule 17 cannot apply before the start as proper course does not exist yet (rule 16.1 still limits her).

q: Rounding the leeward mark in 15 knots you gybe from starboard to port to windward of Black, who is overlapped to leeward of you and gybes too. As your boom comes across the boat rolls, and your boom end swings over Black's deck and touches her mainsheet. No damage. Who broke a rule?
answer: You — as the windward boat you must keep clear, boom included; touching Black is a failure to keep clear (rules 11 and 14)
why: Rule 11 applies throughout a gybe (rule 13 covers only tacking); the windward boat's gear must stay clear of the leeward boat.

figure.note: Your boom swings over Black's deck

ru.Your boom swings over Black's deck: Ваш гик проносится над палубой Чёрной

q: You are overlapped to windward of a Dragon on the same tack on a beat, and she slowly climbs up on you. Your helm says he is already pinching and cannot point any higher, so the leeward boat has to leave him alone. What does the rule require?
answer: You must still keep clear — tack away, slow down or drop astern; rule 11 does not depend on how high you can point
why: Rule 11: the windward boat keeps clear; how she does it is her problem — the leeward boat may sail her course.

figure.note: A is the Dragon, pointing higher than you

q: Three Lasers are overlapped on starboard tack after the start: Red to leeward, you in the middle, White to windward, with half a length between each. Red luffs slowly. White does not respond, so you cannot luff without hitting her, and you touch Red. Who broke a rule?
answer: White broke rule 11 by not keeping clear of you; you are exonerated for touching Red because White compelled you (rule 43.1(a))
why: Rule 11 applies to each pair; a boat compelled to break a rule by another boat's breach is exonerated under rule 43.1(a).

figure.note: Red luffs; White does not respond

q: On a reach you are the leeward boat; Grey is overlapped to windward of you, and Black is overlapped to windward of Grey but her bow is behind your stern. You luff. Black says you may not luff her because she is not overlapped with you. Is she overlapped?
answer: Yes — boats are overlapped when a boat between them overlaps both; Black is a windward boat and must keep clear of you (rule 11)
why: Definition Overlap: boats are also overlapped when a boat between them overlaps both; then rule 11 applies to the windward boat.

q: You are close-hauled on port tack. Blue, also on port, is above you on a reach, footing fast and coming down across your course so that within seconds your bows will be overlapped and she will be the windward boat. Who keeps clear?
answer: Blue — once the boats are on the same tack and overlapped, the windward boat keeps clear, whatever her point of sail (rule 11)
why: Rule 11 depends on tack and overlap only; a reaching boat to windward of a close-hauled boat on the same tack keeps clear.

q: In a handicap race a 40-ft racer-cruiser is overlapped to windward of your Laser on the same tack, both close-hauled, and she is drifting down onto you in a dying breeze. Her crew say that a small dinghy should get out of the way of a big yacht. Who keeps clear?
answer: The big boat — she is the windward boat, and rule 11 does not care about size
why: Rule 11: the windward boat keeps clear; size, class and handicap make no difference.

q: Red is overlapped to windward of you on the same tack with her bow half a length ahead of yours; both of you are close-hauled and your courses slowly converge. Red's helm says that as the boat ahead she has right of way and you must bear away. Is that right?
answer: No — overlapped boats are judged by windward and leeward, not by whose bow is ahead; Red, to windward, keeps clear (rule 11)
why: Definition Overlap: boats are overlapped unless one is clear astern; while overlapped, rule 11 applies, not rule 12.

q: Twenty seconds before the start you and Blue both luff head to wind side by side at the committee boat, having both been on starboard tack; Blue is on your port side. You drift down onto her. Who keeps clear?
answer: You — head to wind you both remain on starboard tack; Blue, on your port (formerly leeward) side, is the leeward boat, so you keep clear (rule 11)
why: Definition Leeward and Windward: head to wind, the leeward side is the one that was leeward before; rule 11 still applies.

q: On a broad reach you are overlapped to windward of Black on the same tack. Black bears away towards the leeward mark, still well outside the zone, and as she turns her stern swings up towards your bow. You hold your course. What are your obligations?
answer: Keep clear — you are the windward boat (rule 11); Black may bear away but must give you room to keep clear (rule 16.1)
why: Rule 11 keeps the duty on the windward boat whatever course the leeward boat sails; rule 16.1 limits how the leeward boat may turn.

figure.note: Black bears away

q: A faster Melges 24 comes up from clear astern and establishes an overlap to windward of you on a reach, a length away. You luff hard at once, well above your proper course, and she has to luff sharply to keep clear. She protests you under rule 17. Who is right?
answer: You — rule 17 limits only a leeward boat that overlapped from astern; you may luff (within rule 16.1) and she keeps clear (rule 11)
why: Rule 17 applies to a boat that became overlapped to leeward from clear astern; here the overlap came from windward, so rule 11 governs.

figure.note: Red is the Melges 24

q: You and Grey are overlapped on port tack, you to leeward, both close-hauled. A starboard-tack boat appears from behind Grey, and you can keep clear of her only by bearing away — but Grey is so close that you would hit her. You hail; Grey does nothing and you have to tack away, losing two lengths. Who broke a rule?
answer: Grey — as the windward boat she had to keep clear of you (rule 11), including giving you room to bear away for the starboard-tack boat
why: Keeping clear includes letting the leeward boat change course; Grey had to keep clear so you could keep clear under rule 10.

figure.note: A is on starboard tack

q: A hundred metres from the finishing line you are overlapped to leeward of White on the same tack, both close-hauled towards the committee boat. You luff her slowly towards head to wind to stop her finishing ahead of you. White says luffing is not allowed on the finishing leg. Who keeps clear?
answer: White — she is the windward boat and keeps clear until she has finished and cleared the line (rule 11); you remain limited by rules 16.1 and 17
why: Rule 11 applies up to the finish; there is no special finishing rule, only the usual limits (16.1, 17) on the leeward boat.

q: In a tacking duel on the last beat the leeward boat sits half a metre off your leeward side, overlapped, both on starboard. You want to tack away but cannot pass head to wind without your stern hitting her. What may you do?
answer: Anything that keeps you clear without touching her — slow down and drop astern, then tack; while overlapped you keep clear (rule 11)
why: Rule 11: the windward boat keeps clear; rule 20 (room to tack) exists only at an obstruction, and a tacking boat has no rights.

figure.note: A is half a metre to leeward

q: An Optimist fleet and a 420 fleet share a course with separate starts. A 420 from the earlier start, already on her second lap, is overlapped to windward of your Optimist on the same tack, converging on you on a beat. Her crew say a different fleet is none of your business. Who keeps clear?
answer: The 420 — Part 2 applies between all boats racing, whatever their fleet; the windward boat keeps clear (rule 11)
why: Rule 11 applies between any two boats racing; a boat on another leg is also limited by rule 23.2 but gains no rights from it.

figure.note: Red is the 420

q: Overlapped to windward of Blue on a reach, you hailed «Starboard!» first, loud and clear, before Blue hailed «Up!». You are both on starboard tack. Blue luffs gently and you have to respond. Does your earlier hail give you any right?
answer: No — hails do not create rights; you are the windward boat and keep clear of Blue (rule 11)
why: Rule 11: between boats on the same tack, the windward boat keeps clear; hailing «Starboard» means nothing here.

q: You are the windward boat, overlapped with Green on starboard tack on a beat, and she is squeezing you up. You decide to keep clear by tacking onto port and passing head to wind in time, without touching her. Was that a lawful way to keep clear?
answer: Yes — the windward boat may keep clear by tacking, as long as she does it without contact; after passing head to wind rule 13 applies to her
why: Rule 11 says keep clear, not how; a tack is fine if clean. Once past head to wind, rule 13 puts the duty on the tacking boat.

figure.note: You begin to tack away

q: In the last ten seconds you are barging at the committee boat: overlapped to windward of Red, both on starboard tack, and there is not enough room for you between Red and the committee boat. Red holds her course and you are squeezed out. Red's crew smile. Who had to keep clear?
answer: You — at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water there is no mark-room, so plain rule 11 applies and the windward boat keeps clear
why: Rule 11 governs; Section C (rule 18) is switched off at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water while boats approach it to start.

q: On a run in a Finn fleet, both on starboard gybe, Yellow is overlapped to leeward of you, having been there since the windward mark. She luffs towards a beam reach to take you up away from the leeward mark. You must gybe away or follow her up. What does rule 11 require of you?
answer: Keep clear in whatever way you choose — respond up or gybe away; Yellow may luff, subject to rules 16.1 and 17
why: Rule 11 applies on every point of sail; the windward boat keeps clear, the leeward boat's luff is limited only by 16.1 and 17.

figure.note: Yellow luffs towards a beam reach

q: You are the leeward boat on starboard and luff Grey, who is overlapped to windward and responds. You keep turning and pass head to wind. What are the rights now?
answer: You are now tacking: you must keep clear of Grey until you are close-hauled on port tack (rule 13); rule 11 no longer applies to her
why: Rule 13: from passing head to wind until close-hauled the tacking boat keeps clear; rules 10–12 are switched off for her.

figure.note: You have just passed head to wind

q: On the run of a 49er regatta in 25 knots you catch a wave and surf straight into the transom of Blue, who is sailing dead ahead of you on the same gybe. Blue did not change course. Who broke a rule?
answer: You — a boat clear astern keeps clear of a boat clear ahead on the same tack (rule 12), and you also broke rule 14
why: Rule 12: on the same tack and not overlapped, the boat clear astern keeps clear; waves are the astern boat's problem.

figure.note: 25 knots, you are surfing down a wave

q: On a reach at a Palma regatta you are a length behind Grey, same tack, and decide to pass her to windward. You luff to go round her stern and your bow clips her transom corner before you are overlapped. Who broke a rule?
answer: You — while clear astern you had to keep clear of Grey (rule 12), and you caused contact (rule 14)
why: Rule 12: until an overlap exists, the boat clear astern keeps clear; the manoeuvre to pass must itself be clear.

q: You are a length clear astern of Red on a reach, same tack, going faster. Red eases her sheets and slows, without altering her heading, so that you close on her transom quickly and have to bear away. You hail that she may not slow down in front of you. Who is right?
answer: Red — she may slow down; rule 16.1 is only about changing course. You, clear astern, keep clear (rule 12)
why: Rule 12 puts the duty on the boat astern; slowing is not a change of course, so rule 16.1 does not apply.

figure.note: Red eases sheets and slows

q: Before the start White is clear ahead of you on starboard tack, half a length away. She luffs smoothly towards head to wind to kill speed. You have room to respond but do not, and you touch her quarter. Who broke a rule?
answer: You — the boat clear astern keeps clear (rule 12); White changed course but gave you room, as rule 16.1 requires
why: Rule 12 applies to the boat astern; the boat ahead may change course if she gives room to keep clear (rule 16.1).

figure.note: White luffs to slow down

q: You have been clear astern of Black on a reach, same tack, keeping clear under rule 12. You sail down to leeward and your bow draws level with her stern, a length away. Black now hails «Keep clear, you're astern!». Which rule applies now?
answer: Rule 11 — you are overlapped and the leeward boat, so Black keeps clear; rules 15 and 17 limit you at first
why: Definition Overlap: once not clear astern, the boats are overlapped and rule 11 applies; rules 15 and 17 limit the new leeward boat.

figure.note: Your bow has just drawn level with her stern

q: On the run you sit directly behind a Dragon on the same gybe, blanketing her, and close in fast. Her helm looks back and shouts that you must not take his wind. Who keeps clear, and may you blanket her?
answer: You keep clear as the boat clear astern (rule 12); taking her wind is allowed
why: Rule 12: the boat clear astern keeps clear; no rule forbids blanketing another boat.

figure.note: A is the Dragon

q: You are clear astern of Blue on a beat, same tack, and pull out to leeward to pass her. At the moment your bow passes her transom, a length to leeward, Blue is pointing slightly below you so that she will converge on you immediately. Contact follows. Who broke a rule?
answer: Probably you — you acquired right of way (rule 11) but had to give Blue room to keep clear at first (rule 15); if you gave her no room, you broke rule 15
why: Rules 12 → 11: the new leeward boat has right of way, but rule 15 requires her to give the windward boat room to keep clear initially.

figure.note: Your bow has just passed Blue's transom to leeward

q: Both of you are running with spinnakers in 20 knots. Red is clear ahead on starboard gybe; you are clear astern on port gybe, surfing faster and about to run up onto her transom. Your crew say you are fine because the boat astern only keeps clear on the same tack. Which rule governs?
answer: Rule 10 — you are on opposite tacks, so the port-tack boat keeps clear; being astern is irrelevant
why: Rule 12 applies only on the same tack; on opposite tacks rule 10 applies regardless of who is ahead.

figure.note: You are on port gybe, Red on starboard

q: Ten seconds before the start Grey sits stalled on the line, sails flapping, close-hauled on starboard but almost stopped. You come in behind her at full speed on starboard, directly astern, and have nowhere to go but into her transom. Who keeps clear?
answer: You — Grey is clear ahead and you are clear astern on the same tack (rule 12); approaching at speed was your choice
why: Rule 12: the boat clear astern keeps clear, however slowly the boat ahead is moving.

figure.note: Grey is almost stopped

q: You are a few metres clear astern of Yellow on a reach, slightly on her leeward quarter and keeping clear. Without warning Yellow bears away sharply across your bow and your bow hits her side; there was no time to react. Who broke a rule?
answer: Yellow — she changed course without giving you room to keep clear (rule 16.1); you are exonerated for breaking rule 12 (rule 43.1(a))
why: Rule 12 keeps the astern boat clear, but a right-of-way boat changing course must give room (16.1); a boat compelled to break a rule is exonerated.

figure.note: Yellow bears away sharply

q: You are clear astern of Blue on a beat and faster; you choose to pass to windward of her. As your bow draws level with her stern you become overlapped to windward. Blue says nothing has changed and you still keep clear. Is she right?
answer: Yes — rule 12 applied while you were astern and rule 11 applies now you are overlapped to windward; either way you keep clear
why: Rules 12 and 11: a boat passing to windward keeps clear throughout — first as clear astern, then as windward boat.

q: You were overlapped to windward of White on a reach and keeping clear. White accelerates in a puff and her stern passes clear ahead of your bow. She then bears away a little across your course, giving you time to react. What are your obligations now?
answer: You are clear astern and keep clear (rule 12); White may change course as long as she gives you room to keep clear (rule 16.1)
why: Definition Overlap: once clear astern, rule 12 replaces rule 11; the boat ahead may change course within rule 16.1.

q: The breeze has died to two knots on a river course and the stream is carrying the fleet along. You are clear astern of Red on the same tack; the current carries you into her transom while neither of you can steer. Did you break a rule?
answer: Yes — clear astern you keep clear (rule 12) and avoid contact (rule 14); the current is no excuse
why: Rule 12 applies whenever boats are racing; rule 14 asks only that contact be avoided «if reasonably possible».

figure.note: Two knots of wind, a strong stream

q: On a reach in a sportsboat fleet you believe you are clear ahead of Green, who is on your leeward quarter. Her bowsprit is extended with the gennaker set, and its tip reaches past your transom although her hull does not. She hails «Leeward boat!». Is she overlapped with you?
answer: Yes — equipment in normal position counts, so her bowsprit creates the overlap; rule 11 applies and you are the windward boat
why: Definition Clear Astern: a boat is clear astern when her hull and equipment in normal position are behind the other's; a set bowsprit counts.

q: On the run you are two lengths clear astern of Black, both on starboard gybe, and keeping clear under rule 12. Black gybes onto port and continues down the leg; you hold your course on starboard and you converge. Who keeps clear now?
answer: Black — after her gybe you are on opposite tacks, so the port-tack boat keeps clear (rule 10); rule 12 no longer applies
why: Rule 12 is a same-tack rule; once the boats are on opposite tacks, rule 10 decides, whoever is ahead.

q: Blue is two lengths clear ahead of you on starboard tack on a beat; you are keeping clear. She tacks onto port right in your path and settles close-hauled a length and a half ahead of you. Who keeps clear during her tack, and who after it?
answer: Blue both times — while tacking she keeps clear under rule 13, and once close-hauled on port she keeps clear of you, on starboard, under rule 10
why: Rule 12 ends when Blue passes head to wind; rule 13 applies during the tack and rule 10 afterwards, since the tacks differ.

q: In a mixed-class club race your 36-ft cruiser-racer is clear astern of an Optimist on the same tack and closing fast on a reach. Your crew assume the little boat will get out of your way. Who keeps clear?
answer: You — the boat clear astern keeps clear of the boat clear ahead (rule 12); the size of the boats is irrelevant
why: Rule 12 puts the duty on the boat astern; there is no rule about size or speed.

figure.note: A is the Optimist

q: You are sailing a length and a half behind Grey on a beat, same tack, a little to leeward of her track. You hail «Leeward boat!» and expect her to hold her course. Grey luffs slightly and you have to luff too. Did Grey have to respect your position?
answer: No — you were clear astern, not overlapped, so you had no rights; you keep clear under rule 12 (Grey must still give you room when she changes course, rule 16.1)
why: Leeward and windward are only defined between overlapped boats; clear astern you keep clear under rule 12.

q: On a reach Black is three lengths ahead of you on the same tack. She luffs twenty degrees to keep her wind clear of your approach, then bears away again. You never need to alter course. Did Black do anything wrong?
answer: No — a boat clear ahead may change course to defend her wind; you, clear astern, simply keep clear (rule 12)
why: Rule 12: clear astern keeps clear; the boat ahead is limited only by rule 16.1, and rule 17 does not restrict a boat clear ahead.

figure.note: Black luffs to defend her wind

q: Red rounds the windward mark just ahead of you and bears away onto the run, but her spinnaker hoist goes wrong and she wallows. You are directly astern on the same tack and closing fast. Who keeps clear?
answer: You — Red is clear ahead and you are clear astern on the same tack (rule 12)
why: Rule 12: whatever is happening on the boat ahead, the boat clear astern keeps clear.

q: On a reaching leg you are clear astern of White and faster. Each time you head down to pass her to leeward she bears away below her proper course to stay between you and the leeward mark; you have to keep clear. You protest that she sailed below her proper course. Will it succeed?
answer: No — there is no longer a rule against a boat sailing below her proper course; White may do so, giving you room to keep clear, and you keep clear under rule 12
why: The old rule against sailing below proper course was deleted in 2013; rule 12 keeps the boat astern clear, rule 16.1 limits the boat ahead.

q: Approaching the finishing line on the same tack, you are half a length clear astern of Blue. Blue luffs slowly head to wind to shoot the line and loses speed; you had room and time to respond but misjudge it and your bow touches her transom. Who broke a rule?
answer: You — the boat clear astern keeps clear (rule 12); Blue changed course slowly enough to give you room (rule 16.1)
why: Rule 12 applies until a boat has finished and cleared the line; a luff that leaves room to keep clear complies with rule 16.1.

q: You are clear astern of Green on a beat and gaining. Green looks back, sees you half a length from her transom and bears away a few degrees to open the gap because she fears a collision. There is no contact. Green protests you. Did you break rule 12?
answer: Yes, if Green's fear was reasonable — keeping clear means she can sail her course without needing to take avoiding action, and she took it
why: Definition Keep Clear: the right-of-way boat must have no need to take avoiding action; a justified avoiding action shows rule 12 was broken.

q: Three boats are in line astern on a reach in 20 knots, a length apart, all on the same tack: A ahead, you in the middle, C behind. C surfs into your transom and pushes you into A. Who broke a rule?
answer: C — she had to keep clear of you (rule 12); you are exonerated for the contact with A because C compelled it (rule 43.1(a))
why: Rule 12 applies to each pair; a boat forced into a breach by another boat's breach is exonerated (rule 43.1(a)).

q: You are a length clear astern of Yellow on a reach, same tack, and clearly faster. You can pass her on either side. Which side gives you right of way once you are overlapped?
answer: To leeward — overlapped to leeward you become the right-of-way boat (rule 11), limited by rules 15 and 17; to windward you keep clear
why: Rules 12 and 11: passing to windward you stay the keep-clear boat; passing to leeward you gain rights, limited by rules 15 and 17.

q: You are close-hauled on starboard tack in an ILCA 7. Red, on port, tacks a length in front of you; she is still turning, sails flapping, and not yet close-hauled on starboard when you have to bear away to miss her. Who broke a rule?
answer: Red — after passing head to wind a boat keeps clear of others until she is on a close-hauled course (rule 13)
why: Rule 13: from passing head to wind until she is on a close-hauled course, a boat keeps clear; rules 10–12 do not apply to her.

q: You and Blue are both close-hauled on port tack, side by side a length apart, Blue on your starboard side. A header comes and you both tack at the same moment; halfway through, both past head to wind, you are converging. Which boat keeps clear?
answer: You — when two boats are tacking at the same time, the one on the other's port side keeps clear (rule 13)
why: Rule 13, last sentence: if two boats are subject to it at the same time, the one on the other's port side or astern keeps clear.

q: Grey is a length and a half clear ahead of you on starboard tack on a beat. She tacks onto port; you tack at the same moment, so that both of you are past head to wind together, you directly astern of her. Who keeps clear while you are both tacking?
answer: You — of two boats tacking at the same time, the one astern keeps clear (rule 13)
why: Rule 13: if two boats are tacking at the same time, the one on the other's port side or the one astern keeps clear.

q: You are close-hauled on starboard. Black, on port, crosses just ahead of your bow and tacks onto your lee bow, completing her tack close-hauled half a length to leeward and slightly ahead of you. You can keep clear by luffing a little, which you do. What are the rights after her tack?
answer: Black is now the leeward boat with right of way (rule 11); she had to keep clear while tacking (rule 13) and give you room to keep clear at first (rule 15), which she did
why: Rule 13 ends when Black is close-hauled; then rule 11 applies, and rule 15 asks only that you have room to keep clear.

answer: White, if your avoiding action was needed as soon as she became close-hauled — she must give you room to keep clear (rule 15); after that you are clear astern and keep clear (rule 12)
why: Rule 13 ends when the tacking boat is close-hauled; rule 12 then applies, but rule 15 obliges her to give the boat astern room initially.

q: You are fetching the windward mark, to be left to port, close-hauled on starboard, well inside the zone. Green comes in on port, tacks under your bow a length from the mark and is still head to wind when you must luff above close-hauled to avoid her. Which rules did Green break?
answer: Rule 13 — she had to keep clear while tacking; and she also broke rule 18.3 by making you sail above close-hauled to avoid her
why: Rule 13 applies to a tacking boat anywhere; at a mark to be left to port, 18.3 adds that she must not make a starboard boat sail above close-hauled.

q: Rounding the leeward mark, Yellow gybes from port to starboard right next to you; you are running on starboard gybe, overlapped to windward of her. As she gybes she claims that, like a boat tacking, she has no obligations while her boom is crossing and you must stay clear. Is she right?
answer: No — rule 13 covers tacking only; a boat gybing keeps whatever obligations she has under rules 10, 11 and 12 throughout

answer: No — rule 17 refers to your own proper course, which may differ from Black's; sailing your fastest course to the gate is not above it
